hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
I would not currently inject gray-market “research peptides.” The sourcing and quality-control risks are simply too high.

The question isn’t whether peptides can work as signaling molecules (they can). It’s whether the vial contains the peptide it claims, at the stated dose, without microbial contamination, endotoxins, heavy metals, or peptide-related impurities.

The FDA does not verify the safety, effectiveness, or quality of compounded drugs before marketing. Does that mean every compounded product is unsafe? No. But the safeguards are different.

Until a specific research peptide has credible human evidence and a reliable source with transparent, independent testing, I would hold off.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Bone health deserves attention before menopause, not just after.

Roughly two-thirds of bone lost across the menopausal transition tends to occur within a three-year window - from one year before to two years after the final menstrual period.

In a study of 862 women, bone density at the spine fell 10.6% over 10 years, but 7.4% was lost during this brief “transmenopause” period. Bone density of the femur fell 9.1%, with 5.8% lost during the same window.

This is a reason for women to prioritize resistance and high-impact training around the menopause transition to prevent or slow the loss of bone density.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Women with a history of menopausal hormone therapy had 2.5% greater grip strength at ages 60-64 than women who had never used it. Among women 80 and older, that gap was 14.3%.

Activity patterns added an interesting layer. Among women 65 and older, those with a history of hormone therapy and intermediate amounts of moderate-intensity physical activity had 16% greater grip strength, while those who were the most sedentary still had 14% greater grip strength if they'd undergone hormone therapy vs. not.

Menopausal hormone therapy may help preserve strength into later life, including among women who aren't very active. But of course, regular activity is crucial for strength preservation and should be done regardless of whether or not someone is on hormone therapy.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
I've been hearing people say glucose spikes don't matter as long as your average blood sugar looks fine. Your brain may disagree.

Researchers put continuous glucose monitors on older adults for three days and then scanned their brains. The people whose glucose swung up and down the most over 30 minutes to 2 hours had less gray matter in the hippocampus (the brain's memory center) and did worse on cognitive tests. That held even after accounting for HbA1c (the three-month blood sugar average most doctors check).

A normal average can hide plenty of spikes and crashes. I'd pay attention to what happens after meals, not just the number on your lab report. Ideally, keep the swings small. And really only a CGM can tell you this.

hits.name: Mark Hyman, M.D.
Andy Galpin, PhD
hits.text:
Why wouldn't you want your testosterone as high as possible? Dr. Ben House has a good answer.

High testosterone upregulates EPO, which tells your body to make more red blood cells. More red blood cells means more viscous blood. You're not pumping blood anymore, you're pumping oil.

Now add left ventricular hypertrophy. The heart wall thickens, and it's pushing against more back pressure with every beat.

As Ben puts it, your heart is pumping ketchup against a bunch of extra muscle.

You don't want to run that for decades, assuming you get decades.
hits.draft_en:
Galpin’s guest puts it blunt: max testosterone isn’t automatically max health.

High T can push thicker blood and a thicker heart wall — “pumping ketchup” against extra muscle. Not a badge for decades.

Over 50, chase sleep, training, waistline, and honest labs with a GP — not a race to the top number on a printout.
hits.video_tip: 25–30s face-to-cam; caption “not max labs — smart labs.”

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
It’s a reality of aging that we need more dietary protein to keep muscle mass. If you're over 65, the source of your protein may matter as much as the amount.

Researchers gave older adults two meals with the same amount of protein and the same calories. One was built around beef, and the other was vegan. After the beef meal, muscle protein synthesis was about 47% higher. After the vegan meal, it barely moved from where it was before eating (PMID 37972895).

As we age, muscle gets harder to build and easier to lose. We need to make high-quality animal protein the anchor of every meal.
hits.draft_en:
Bikman’s point for older bodies: you need more protein — and the source can matter as much as the grams.

Same calories, same protein count: beef meal lifted muscle protein synthesis about 47%; the vegan meal barely moved the needle in that study.

Over 50 on tools, don’t leave muscle to chance. Anchor the plate with real animal protein.
hits.video_tip: 20s steak/eggs on a plate then a thumbs-up; caption “anchor the meal.”

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Exercise slowed epigenetic aging on two DNA-methylation clocks in breast cancer survivors.

During the first 6 months of the 12-month study, epigenetic aging halted in the exercise group while controls aged at twice the chronological rate, even though the intervention added only about 6 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per day!

Faster epigenetic aging was also associated with worse attention and self-reported cognition, and some methylation changes implicated BDNF signaling as a plausible link to neuroplasticity.

This suggests some aging signatures after cancer treatment appear to be responsive to movement, even when the added activity isn't enormous.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda’s data: in survivors, exercise basically paused epigenetic aging while controls aged twice as fast — and the extra work was only about six minutes a day of harder movement.

Six minutes isn’t a marathon. It’s a deliberate block.

If your week is dusty and heavy already, protect a short hard bit on purpose. If it’s a soft week, don’t wait for perfect — move.
hits.video_tip: 20–25s brisk walk or step-ups; caption “six hard minutes.”

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Retatrutide has an advantage over other GLP-1-based drugs, and I think it comes down to glucagon, one of the more overlooked hormones in metabolism.

Retatrutide adds glucagon on top of the GLP-1 and GIP signals. In the newly-released phase 3 TRIUMPH-1 trial, just published in NEJM (NCT05929066), adults with obesity took it for 80 weeks. At the top dose, people lost 25% of their body weight on average. More than a third lost at least 30%. Fasting insulin fell by more than half, something I always focus on, and over 90% of people with prediabetes ended up with normal blood sugar.

Insulin tells the body to store fuel, and glucagon tells the body to burn it. In a separate study, researchers raised glucagon to normal physiological levels and found that the liver's mitochondria burned fuel 50 to 75% faster (PMID 39197461). In another study, a glucagon infusion raised energy expenditure by about 15% (PMID 26434748). 

Ideally, if you take it, protect your fat-free mass with resistance exercise and abundant protein and natural fats. I also feel strongly that any of these drugs needs to be viewed as a temporary crutch--use it to develop new habits (i.e., control carbs) and then taper off.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Moms (to be): your metabolism matters. It may shape your child's mental health for decades.

In a Danish study of 2.4 million births followed for up to almost 40 years, children whose mothers had diabetes during pregnancy were 15% more likely to be diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder. Their risk of schizophrenia was 55% higher, and anxiety, intellectual disability and behavioral disorders were also more common.

Mom's blood sugar crosses the placenta, and the baby's pancreas answers by making more insulin. A developing brain grows in whatever metabolic environment mom provides.

outsiders.name: GeLun Ding
outsiders.text:
Manus is truly the saddest story in the AI circle. Last December, Meta spent $2 billion to acquire Manus, when Manus was still widely recognized as the leader among Agents. But just 4 months later, China demanded that Meta cancel this acquisition. By June this year, Meta sold Manus back to a group of Chinese companies for almost $2 billion. Then last week, Zuckerberg directly released Meta's own AI Agent—Muse, which is now considered by many to be the leader in consumer-grade AI Agents. In other words, Meta essentially got all of Manus's IP for free, slapped a new name on it, added a cute character, and relaunched Manus.

This is really pretty tragic. Manus 2.0 was just released yesterday, but it seems like hardly anyone cares. Right now, there's actually no real reason to keep using Manus, especially since it still has a bunch of data security risks. Muse has stolen all the spotlight, and it even directly gives every user their own VM. If Manus doesn't quickly pivot to do something else, you could basically say it's done for.

Come for talks, workshops, and office hours with our team, plus time to meet others building with Claude. Whether you're a founder, a CEO, or a builder, there's a session for you.

virals.text:
Biosecurity is one of the most urgent challenges for the AI era. Bringing SynthID to biology so AI-generated proteins can be watermarked is a critical step - and we’re open sourcing SynthID Bio tools so the research community can build on this work. Published in 
@Nature
 today, congrats to the team!
